Heritage walk · Madhya Pradesh

Heritage walk in Bhopal: old city, lakes and nearby sites

A heritage walk in Bhopal covers the old city of the Begums: Taj-ul-Masajid, Gauhar Mahal, Moti Masjid, the Chowk markets and the Upper Lake. Bhopal is also the base for three of central India's major sites within about two hours: Sanchi, Bhimbetka and Bhojpur, plus Udayagiri near Vidisha.

We arrange heritage walks in Bhopal and trips to Sanchi, Bhimbetka and Bhojpur on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi.

Why Bhopal matters for heritage

Bhopal is rarely on lists of India's great heritage cities, yet few places put so much within reach. Two UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the Buddhist monuments at Sanchi (1989) and the rock shelters of Bhimbetka (2003), are within about 50 to 70 kilometres. The unfinished Bhojeshwar temple at Bhojpur, the Gupta-period caves at Udayagiri and the hill fort at Raisen are close too. A school or college group can cover tens of thousands of years of Indian history in three or four days from one hotel.

The city itself has a distinctive story. For more than a century, from 1819 to 1926, Bhopal state was ruled by a line of women, the Begums of Bhopal, who built mosques, palaces, schools and waterworks. Old Bhopal still has their markets, gateways and buildings, and two of the best museums in central India are in the newer city.

Layers of history around Bhopal

The deepest layer is prehistoric. The rock shelters at Bhimbetka hold paintings from the Mesolithic onward, with some shelters used far earlier, and are covered in our guide to rock art in India. The Bhimbetka visit looks at how archaeologists sort the layers of painting.

Sanchi's Great Stupa goes back to the Mauryan period in the 3rd century BCE, with its stone casing and four carved gateways added mainly in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE. Nearby, the Udayagiri caves near Vidisha were cut in the early 5th century CE under the Guptas, and include the large Varaha panel. These sites connect directly to the story of the Mauryan empire and Gupta empire.

The name Bhopal is traditionally linked to Raja Bhoja of the Paramara dynasty (11th century), who is credited with the great tank that became the Upper Lake and with the Bhojeshwar temple at Bhojpur, left unfinished with its building ramps still visible. The modern city was founded in the early 18th century by Dost Mohammad Khan, an Afghan soldier. The Begums ruled from 1819, followed by Nawab Hamidullah Khan until the state merged with India in 1949.

Places a heritage walk in Bhopal covers

  1. Taj-ul-Masajid Begun under Shah Jahan Begum (ruled 1868 to 1901), completed 1985

    Huge mosque with pink sandstone facade and white domes; look at the courtyard tank and the long construction history.

  2. Moti Masjid 1860

    Built by Sikandar Begum; a smaller mosque whose design echoes the Jama Masjid of Delhi.

  3. Jama Masjid, Bhopal 1830s

    Built by Qudsia Begum, with gilded spikes on its minarets, in the middle of the Chowk.

  4. Chowk Bazaar 19th century onward

    Old market lanes known for zari work, beaded purses and silver.

  5. Gauhar Mahal 1820s

    Palace of Qudsia Begum on the Upper Lake, mixing Hindu and Mughal elements.

  6. Shaukat Mahal and Sadar Manzil 19th century

    Facades in a mix of European and Indo-Islamic styles at the entrance to the Chowk.

  7. Upper Lake (Bada Talab) Tradition links it to Raja Bhoja, 11th century

    The large tank that shaped the city; the Kamla Park side gives the best view.

  8. Bhojpur Bhojeshwar Temple 11th century

    Unfinished Paramara temple with a huge linga and an ancient construction ramp; vehicle needed.

  9. Bhimbetka Rock Shelters Paleolithic use; paintings from about the Mesolithic onward

    UNESCO site with hundreds of painted shelters; vehicle needed.

  10. Sanchi Stupas 3rd century BCE to 12th century CE

    Great Stupa, gateways, temples and monasteries on a hill; UNESCO site; vehicle needed.

  11. Udayagiri Caves Early 5th century CE

    Gupta-period rock-cut shrines near Vidisha, including the Varaha panel; vehicle needed.

  12. Raisen Fort Medieval, with later additions

    Hilltop fort with tanks, palaces and long walls on the road to Sanchi; vehicle needed.

Walking routes in Bhopal

Old Bhopal on foot

About 2.5 hours

Taj-ul-Masajid → Moti Masjid → Jama Masjid, Bhopal → Chowk Bazaar → Shaukat Mahal and Sadar Manzil → Gauhar Mahal → Upper Lake (Bada Talab)

Rock art and stone (vehicle needed)

A full day

Bhimbetka Rock Shelters → Bhojpur Bhojeshwar Temple

Sanchi, Vidisha and Raisen (vehicle needed)

One long day or two days

Raisen Fort → Sanchi Stupas → Udayagiri Caves

Museums in Bhopal

  • Madhya Pradesh Tribal Museum. Large galleries made with artists from the state's tribal communities, on homes, ritual, games and crafts.
  • State Museum, Bhopal. Sculpture, bronzes, coins and inscriptions from across Madhya Pradesh, with a fine gallery of Jain and Brahmanical images.
  • Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya. Open-air anthropology museum on the Shamla Hills with full-size houses from across India.
  • Archaeological Museum, Sanchi. ASI site museum with the lion capital of the Ashokan pillar and sculpture from the stupas.

Best time for a walk

October to March. The monsoon (July to September) is green but paths at Bhimbetka can be slippery, and summer is very hot.

What you see on a walk in old Bhopal

The old city walk starts at Taj-ul-Masajid, one of the largest mosques in India, begun under Shah Jahan Begum in the late 19th century and completed only in the 1980s. It continues through the Chowk market with its lanes of zari, batua (beadwork purses) and silver, to Moti Masjid (1860, built by Sikandar Begum), Gauhar Mahal (1820s, built for Qudsia Begum) on the lake shore, and the Shaukat Mahal facade with its mix of European and Indo-Islamic styles.

The theme of the walk is water and city identity: how the Upper and Lower lakes shaped where palaces and markets were built, and how the city still depends on them. Our Old Bhopal walk is built around this. Those interested in a single building can take the Taj-ul-Masajid visit, which also looks at what it means to visit a mosque that is a working place of worship.

Day trips from Bhopal: Sanchi, Bhimbetka, Bhojpur and more

All of these need a vehicle. Bhimbetka and Bhojpur lie south of the city and pair well in one day, which is the logic of the Bhimbetka and Bhojpur day. Sanchi is north-east, about 45 kilometres, and combines with Udayagiri and Vidisha; the two-day Sanchi and Vidisha immersion allows time for the museum and the smaller stupas. Raisen Fort is on the way to Sanchi.

For a longer study tour, Central India: rock art and Buddhist archaeology links all of these with an archaeologist over several days, and Mandu, further west near Indore, adds a Sultanate hill capital.

Bhopal heritage walk for schools and groups

Old Bhopal is compact but has steep, busy lanes, so groups of more than 30 are best split. Mornings are calmest in the market. Taj-ul-Masajid is closed to visitors at prayer times, so plan around them, and dress modestly. The Tribal Museum and State Museum make a good indoor afternoon, and the Tribal Museum session teaches students how to read objects rather than only labels.

Bhimbetka involves walking on rocky paths between shelters; Sanchi involves a gentle hill climb. Both are fine for most school groups. Talaash Heritage arranges any combination on request, often beginning with a classroom lecture before the trip.

Questions people ask

What are the main historical places in Bhopal?

In the city: Taj-ul-Masajid, Moti Masjid, the Jama Masjid, Gauhar Mahal, the Chowk and the Upper Lake. Nearby: Sanchi, Bhimbetka, Bhojpur, Udayagiri and Raisen Fort, all reachable as day trips by road.

How far are Sanchi and Bhimbetka from Bhopal?

Sanchi is about 45 kilometres north-east of Bhopal and Bhimbetka about 45 to 50 kilometres south. Each is roughly an hour to an hour and a half by road, depending on traffic.

Which museums in Bhopal are worth visiting with students?

The Madhya Pradesh Tribal Museum, the State Museum and the open-air Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya. Together they cover anthropology, archaeology and art, and each can fill half a day.

Can a school do Bhopal heritage in one trip?

Yes. A three-day plan works well: old Bhopal and the museums on day one, Bhimbetka and Bhojpur on day two, and Sanchi with Udayagiri on day three. A vehicle is needed for days two and three.

Who were the Begums of Bhopal?

Four women who ruled Bhopal state between 1819 and 1926: Qudsia Begum, Sikandar Begum, Shah Jahan Begum and Sultan Jahan Begum. They built mosques, palaces and public institutions that still shape the old city.
